Demure

/dih-MYOOR/ - rhymes with pure · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Demure means quiet, modest, and reserved.

The new hire is demure in meetings — hands folded, questions saved for email — and merciless at the Friday crossword.

Worked Example

The 1908 etiquette manual devotes a full chapter to the demure entrance: eyes level but soft, voice pitched low, opinions offered only when asked twice. What it teaches is not shyness — the manual is plain that a hostess must never seem afraid of her own parlor — but a chosen smallness of manner, composure worn like a well-cut coat.

Demure is the exact word for that manner, because it means quiet, modest, and reserved — with the calm underneath doing the real work. A demure person is not hiding or trembling; she has set her own volume low on purpose. Shy names what someone cannot help; demure names what someone chooses.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

soft-spoken: volume only; demure covers the whole manner

retiring: shrinks from notice; the demure person is present, just quiet about it

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

showy: performs for every eye in the room

brash: loud, bold, and unembarrassed

Where it sits · how far the person retreats from company — quiet → demure → withdrawn

quiet vs. demure: Quiet counts decibels and nothing else — a quiet person may still argue you flat in a whisper.

withdrawn vs. demure: Withdrawn goes further than demure — the demure guest is at the table, composed and pleasant; the withdrawn one has left the conversation while still in the chair.

Build the Word

The pieces

Root — demure

Root — demure: borrowed whole from Old French

Put it together

Put it together: There is nothing to peel off here. Demure arrived in English whole, from Old French, in the 1300s — probably from demorer, "to stay, to remain" (a settled, stays-put manner), though some trace it to meur, "ripe, fully grown." Either way, English never built it from de- plus anything: the de- you see is a fossil of French, not this unit's prefix at work.

Why there's no relative to spot

Why there's no relative to spot: Whichever French verb demure came from, its family stayed behind in France — no English relative survives to compare it with. Learn the manner it names directly: quiet, composed, and choosing to be both.

Strength Check

Word Choice

neutral / a little old-fashioned

Demure is approving or gently teasing, never harsh, and it mostly describes manner — a demure reply, a demure bow. Shy is the involuntary cousin; soft-spoken measures only volume. It is also this unit's quietest impostor: the de- is French furniture, not the prefix, and nothing about a demure person has been lowered — the composure is the whole point.
